The company is deepening its infrastructure push through AI factories, its DSX platform, and global data center partnerships. Nvidia is also expanding into robotics and space computing, betting that accelerated computing can scale far beyond data centers. **Nvidia**(NASDAQ: NVDA) has become one of the biggest names in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, but what matters now is what comes next. Five years is a long time in tech, and Nvidia still has huge plans in its pipeline, spanning AI infrastructure, robotics, and more. "Act 2" is the global rollout. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # Build a Multi-Model AI Router: Fallback in 13 Steps [2026] * [![Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/)[Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/ "Posts by Marcus Chen") * [AI & Machine Learning](https://tech-insider.org/category/ai-machine-learning/) [Marcus Chen](https://tech-insider.org/author/marcus-chen/) September 25, 2026 22 min read Four major AI labs shipped new flagship models inside the same three-week window this September: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s [Claude Fable](https://tech-insider.org/claude-fable-5-1-api-setup-2026/) 5.1 (and the access-restricted Claude Mythos 5.1), Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash, and DeepSeek’s open-weight V4.1 Flash. That pace is exactly why a growing number of engineering teams stopped hardcoding a single provider into their apps. When a model gets rate-limited, drops a benchmark lead to a rival released two weeks later, or triples in price after a promo ends, an app wired to one API has no fallback plan. This tutorial walks through building your own multi-model AI router with automatic fallback, using the open-source LiteLLM library as the base, so a single outage or rate-limit spike never takes your product down. By the end you’ll have a working proxy server that can call GPT-6 Astra first, fall back to Claude Fable 5.1 if OpenAI throttles you, and drop to a cheaper model like Gemini 3.8 Flash or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for high-volume, low-stakes requests, all from one consistent API your application code never has to change. None of this is theoretical plumbing. Any team that shipped a product against a single provider’s chat completions endpoint this year has probably already lived through at least one of three scenarios: a sudden 429 rate-limit wall during a traffic spike, a multi-hour partial outage documented on that provider’s public status page, or a pricing change that made last month’s cost model obsolete overnight. A router doesn’t prevent any of those events. highlights.content: **[Help Net Security newsletters](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)**: Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – **[subscribe here!](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)** ![](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/24100957/2026-95-cis-l-hi.jpg) ![Industry News](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/09100818/padlock-100x100.png) # Dataiku Agent Management reveals unmonitored AI agents [Dataiku](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/tag/dataiku/) has announced the launch of Agent Management, a standalone product that finds every [AI agent](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/09/16/google-mandiant-enterprise-ai-security-risks-report/) an enterprise is running, regardless of which platform built it, measures the business and technical performance, and flags agents that pose the greatest risk. ![Dataiku Agent Management](https://img2.helpnetsecurity.com/posts2026/Dataiku-Agent_Management_Inventory.webp "inventory") ![Dataiku Agent Management](https://img2.helpnetsecurity.com/posts2026/Dataiku-Agent_Management_Inventory.webp "inventory") The launch addresses a disconnect between how fast agents are being created and adopted and organizations’ ability to observe and manage them. Every large company already keeps an account of the software it runs: who owns it, what it costs, and when it renews. Almost none can say the same about the AI agents. In fact, fewer than one in five organizations maintain a complete, current inventory of their AI systems, according to IBM’s “AI in Motion” research. The reason is that most agent platforms can only see the agents built on them, leaving the bulk of a company’s agent estate without clear ownership, purpose, risk, or business outcome. “Ask a bank how many servers it runs, and you get an answer to the decimal. Ask how many AI agents it’s running, and you get a shrug or a guess,” said [Florian Douetteau](https://www.linkedin.com/in/fdouetteau/), CEO of Dataiku. “Nobody set out to build it this way. Teams built agents faster than anyone could count them. Agent Management tells you what’s actually out there, and what it’s actually worth.” Agent Management connects to the platforms that enterprise teams already use to run agents, including AWS Bedrock, Databricks Agents, Google Vertex, Microsoft Copilot Studio and Azure Foundry, Salesforce Agentforce, Snowflake Cortex, Dataiku itself, with OpenTelemetry support for custom environments, and scans them into a single inventory. It automatically identifies each agent’s structure, including the tools and models it relies on, giving supervisors full transparency into how an agent actually works, not just that it exists. For the highest-risk agents, the ones handling customers, sensitive data, or live transactions, it keeps a standing record of certification status, named risks, and tests that rerun on a schedule, so the evidence trail already exists when a manager, auditor, or regulator asks for it. Unlike traditional agent monitoring capabilities, which are in a single vendor’s stack and designed to favor that vendor’s own agents, Agent Management is deliberately agnostic. It sits above the stack, which lets it answer questions no single platform can, which agents are unmonitored, where risk is concentrated, and which ones earn their cost. Teams ask those questions in plain language and get an answer covering the whole portfolio. ![Add Help Net Security as a preferred source on Google](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/themes/hns26/assets/images/social/google_preferred_source_badge_dark_en.png) ## **Featured** news ![](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/24100954/2026-95-cis-r-hi.jpg) ## ****Resources**** ## **Don't** miss ![](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/24082040/2026-95-cis-welchi.webp)

[SEO](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/category/seo/) # Google Has Deployed A New AI Spam Detector Called SAFE Google published details of it's new anti-spam system designed to detect AI content. This is why it may be a part of Google's Spam Update. ![Google Has Deployed A New AI Spam Detector Called SAFE](https://cdn.searchenginejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/google-ai-spam-agents-192.jpg) Google has published a research paper about detecting spam that mimics a human manual review that catches content that violates the “spirit” of policy violations and platform guidelines. The system is called Scaled Abuse Forensics Examiner (SAFE) and it is expressly designed to identify AI-generated content. ## Google Is Focusing On AI Slop This is Google’s second system identified in 2026 that is designed to catch AI-generated spam. The previously identified system is called [Scalable Cluster Termination System (S-CTS](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-generated-ai-detected/579987/)). The fact that Google is devoting resources to catching AI slop shows that Google is concerned about AI spam content these systems may be a component of the [September Spam update](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-september-2026-spam-update/590828/). AI enables abusive networks to mass-produce synthetic content while systematically tweaking it to evade traditional detection systems. Humans can find coordinated spam networks by examining relationships, behavior, content, and even zoom out to examine infrastructure but manual inspections don’t scale fast enough to catch up with the massive scale of AI-generated slop. This new system is designed to close that gap. The research paper is titled, *The Synthetic Gap: Automating Forensic Investigation of “AI Slop” with the Scaled Abuse* *Forensics Examiner (SAFE).* The research paper [explains](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/1039292.pdf): > “Traditional forensic workflows, which rely heavily on manual pattern recognition and metadata analysis, are ill-equipped to handle this volume. The “synthetic gap”—the time between the emergence of a new generative attack vector and the deployment of a counter-measure remains a critical vulnerability.” ## Identifies Spirit Of Policy Violations The paper says SAFE identifies “spirit of policy” violations primarily with a few-shot-trained LLM. The goal of SAFE is to catch content that may not match an existing rule or known violation pattern but still violates the intent of the policy or platform guideline and can go undetected by traditional classifiers and fine-tuned violation-detection models. ## The SAFE System Has Been Deployed The research paper is very secretive, it’s only three pages long, and mentions having tested the system but does not share the results of the tests. That is highly unusual and points to how Google is keeping the public in the dark about SAFE. The launch reinforces Veeva's push to embed AI across its life sciences software suite while helping customers streamline study setup using standardized workflows. The announcement strengthens Veeva's broader strategy of deepening the value of its Clinical Data ecosystem rather than launching a standalone paid product. By making the agent part of its electronic data capture (EDC) offering with no additional license, Veeva aims to drive adoption, improve customer efficiency and further differentiate its platform. This could support long-term customer retention and reinforce its competitive position in the clinical trial technology market. **Likely Trend of VEEV Stock Following the News** Following the announcement, shares of VEEV traded flat in yesterday’s trading. The launch of Study Builder Agent is likely to strengthen Veeva's long-term growth by making its Clinical Data platform more valuable and harder for customers to replace. By enabling sponsors to configure studies much faster using their existing standards and the CDISC Unified Study Definitions Model (USDM), the AI agent can reduce manual effort, improve consistency and shorten study startup timelines. Study Builder Agent is embedded within Veeva EDC and Data Quality System (DQS) rather than offered as a separate product. It is positioned to drive broader platform adoption, reinforce customer retention and expand the strategic importance of Veeva's connected clinical ecosystem, supporting durable revenue growth over time. Beyond study setup, the agent automates testing and generates test data, helping organizations validate builds more efficiently and produce audit-ready outputs with minimal deviation from established standards. highlights.content: UPDATED 14:42 EDT / SEPTEMBER 25 2026 ### Closing the gap between your AI eyes and stomach at HumanX GUEST COLUMN by Jason Bloomberg Fresh off my jaunt to AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe last week, I headed back to Amsterdam for the first European installment of the artificial intelligence-focused HumanX conference so I could meet with another round of AI startups. As always, my goal was to uncover the untold stories of innovation across the software landscape – and HumanX Amsterdam 2026 didn’t disappoint. Despite all the crazy hype around AI these days, I found several vendors that were laser-focused on delivering differentiated business value with their innovations, with the goal of helping their customer base move forward with their AI initiatives. In other words, the 10 vendors below are driving their customers to close the gap between their eyes (desire for AI) and their stomachs (their ability to deploy real solutions into production). Here is my list, in alphabetical order: 8wave Oy offers a platform that connects all of an organization’s AI activities by tracking the lineage of the underlying data feeding the various AI applications. The result is “enterprise resource planning or ERP for AI operations” that connects AI activities to the key performance indicators or KPIs important to the business. 8wave’s key innovation: The company has updated the notion of data lineage to “AI lineage,” connecting underlying data to the organization’s core business drivers via AI. Bosun B.V. leverages AI to automate software maintenance across legacy codebases, supporting security fixes, dependency updates and some legacy migration activities. The company tracks the behavior of each legacy asset with a parity file that enables the organization to compare the behavior of the original and updated applications. Bosun’s key innovation: the parity file tracks the behavior of each legacy application via its inputs and outputs in a human-readable and modifiable format that enables organizations to move forward with patches and updates while lowering the risk of breaking something. Clarifeye SAS offers an “AI consultant” that conducts interviews with experts across an organization to collect the tribal knowledge locked in people’s heads. It then combines this knowledge with other sources of information across to help companies build process maps, business rules and playbooks that accurately represent the actual behaviors of the business. Clarifeye’s key innovation: Many AI platforms today can extract information from digital sources like documents, databases, applications and the like. Clarifeye complements these sources of information with the hard-to-reach tribal knowledge that represents how businesses actually operate. Every large company already keeps an account of the software it runs: who owns it, what it costs, and when it renews. Almost none can say the same about the AI agents. In fact, fewer than one in five organizations maintain a complete, current inventory of their AI systems, according to IBM’s “AI in Motion” research. The reason is that most agent platforms can only see the agents built on them, leaving the bulk of a company’s agent estate without clear ownership, purpose, risk, or business outcome. “Ask a bank how many servers it runs, and you get an answer to the decimal. Ask how many AI agents it’s running, and you get a shrug or a guess,” said [Florian Douetteau](https://www.linkedin.com/in/fdouetteau/), CEO of Dataiku. “Nobody set out to build it this way. Teams built agents faster than anyone could count them. Agent Management tells you what’s actually out there, and what it’s actually worth.” Agent Management connects to the platforms that enterprise teams already use to run agents, including AWS Bedrock, Databricks Agents, Google Vertex, Microsoft Copilot Studio and Azure Foundry, Salesforce Agentforce, Snowflake Cortex, Dataiku itself, with OpenTelemetry support for custom environments, and scans them into a single inventory. It automatically identifies each agent’s structure, including the tools and models it relies on, giving supervisors full transparency into how an agent actually works, not just that it exists. For the highest-risk agents, the ones handling customers, sensitive data, or live transactions, it keeps a standing record of certification status, named risks, and tests that rerun on a schedule, so the evidence trail already exists when a manager, auditor, or regulator asks for it. Unlike traditional agent monitoring capabilities, which are in a single vendor’s stack and designed to favor that vendor’s own agents, Agent Management is deliberately agnostic. It sits above the stack, which lets it answer questions no single platform can, which agents are unmonitored, where risk is concentrated, and which ones earn their cost. This is why it may be a part of Google's Spam Update. ![Google Has Deployed A New AI Spam Detector Called SAFE](https://cdn.searchenginejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/google-ai-spam-agents-192.jpg) Google has published a research paper about detecting spam that mimics a human manual review that catches content that violates the “spirit” of policy violations and platform guidelines. The system is called Scaled Abuse Forensics Examiner (SAFE) and it is expressly designed to identify AI-generated content. ## Google Is Focusing On AI Slop This is Google’s second system identified in 2026 that is designed to catch AI-generated spam. The previously identified system is called [Scalable Cluster Termination System (S-CTS](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-generated-ai-detected/579987/)). The fact that Google is devoting resources to catching AI slop shows that Google is concerned about AI spam content these systems may be a component of the [September Spam update](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-september-2026-spam-update/590828/). AI enables abusive networks to mass-produce synthetic content while systematically tweaking it to evade traditional detection systems. Humans can find coordinated spam networks by examining relationships, behavior, content, and even zoom out to examine infrastructure but manual inspections don’t scale fast enough to catch up with the massive scale of AI-generated slop. This new system is designed to close that gap. The research paper is titled, *The Synthetic Gap: Automating Forensic Investigation of “AI Slop” with the Scaled Abuse* *Forensics Examiner (SAFE).* The research paper [explains](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/1039292.pdf): > “Traditional forensic workflows, which rely heavily on manual pattern recognition and metadata analysis, are ill-equipped to handle this volume. The “synthetic gap”—the time between the emergence of a new generative attack vector and the deployment of a counter-measure remains a critical vulnerability.” ## Identifies Spirit Of Policy Violations The paper says SAFE identifies “spirit of policy” violations primarily with a few-shot-trained LLM. The goal of SAFE is to catch content that may not match an existing rule or known violation pattern but still violates the intent of the policy or platform guideline and can go undetected by traditional classifiers and fine-tuned violation-detection models. ## The SAFE System Has Been Deployed The research paper is very secretive, it’s only three pages long, and mentions having tested the system but does not share the results of the tests. [Submit an Article](https://write.insightmediagroup.io) [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/towards-data-science/)[X](https://x.com/TDataScience) [Agentic AI](/category/artificial-intelligence/agentic-ai/) # Jev vs. LLMs: When AI moves from Generation to Decision-making I tested TypeSafe AI’s Jev on 3,080 classification tasks to see how its accuracy, latency, calibration, and confidence compare with LLMs — and whether it works as a practical decision layer for AI systems. [Nhu Hoang](/author/hoanganhquynhnhu/) September 25, 202625 min read ![](https://assets.insightmediagroup.io/media/1789986681697_672yhm.jpg) Photo by [lan deng](https://unsplash.com/@landall?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/assorted-color-succulent-plants-CFKwL570ZSc?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText) ## 1. Before the LLM writes anything ### 1.1 What is Jev? Most AI applications do not always need another paragraph of generated text. Sometimes they just need a decision. Let's imagine opening a support inbox at 9 a.m. and finding 340 new messages. Before anyone writes a reply, the system may need to decide which team should handle the message, whether it is urgent, or whether the customer is asking for a refund. The same pattern shows up in AI agents: before calling a tool, the system may first need to decide whether that action is safe. This is where **Jev** gets interesting. Released by TypeSafe AI in September 2026, Jev is presented as a **System One model**: not a replacement for large language models, but a **more specialized layer for fast, structured decisions** (ex: tool calls). Instead of generating a sentence and then asking software to interpret it, Jev returns a choice from a predefined set of answers together with probabilities. That puts it in a different part of the AI stack. LLMs are good at open-ended language, explanation, and reasoning. Jev is aimed at the **many smaller decisions** surrounding that work: classification, routing, filtering, safety checks, and other tasks where the output is known in advance. ### 1.2 Why I wanted to test it There are already plenty of ways to solve these problems. Rules are fast and cheap, but they become brittle as language changes. Traditional classifiers can be accurate, but they require labelled training data and retraining when the task changes. And an LLM can usually return the answer as JSON, although that means using a generative model for a task that may only require choosing between a few options. The early results around Jev were what caught my attention. In a 400-item PriorBench classification test, **Jev scored 95.9% compared with 77.2% for keyword rules**. In another test published by Dan Shipper's [Every.to](http://Every.to), Jev took a median of **0.35 seconds per passage check, versus 8.83 seconds for Fable 5.1** at high effort. Those numbers come from specific benchmarks, so I would not treat them as universal comparisons—but they were enough to make me curious. There is also the question of confidence. If an LLM writes “I am 90% sure,” how often is it actually right? In Supa Journal's Japanese benchmark on 18 September 2026, four chat models had confidence errors of 0.078–0.163 on a scale from 0 to 1, compared with 0.002–0.047 for Jev. I will explain how that error is measured later, because the meaning of these numbers matters as much as the speed. I was particularly interested in the confidence scores. Jev does not just return a label; it gives probabilities for the available choices. That raises a more useful question than raw accuracy: **when the model says it is confident, can you actually trust that confidence?** So I decided to test it myself. LLMs.content: [Skip to the content](#content) [MIXED Reality News![MIXED Reality News](/resources/logos/logo_mxd_full_light.svg)](https://mixed-news.com/en/ "MIXED Reality News") Virtual Reality News & Augmented Reality News [AI research](https://mixed-news.com/en/artificial-intelligence-news/ai-research/) [0](https://mixed-news.com/en/forecasting-research-institute-leap-ai-expert-accuracy/#comments) # 339 AI experts gave four AI benchmark results a 24.6% chance, superforecasters 9.7% [Michael Zelich](https://mixed-news.com/en/author/michael-zelich/ "Posts by Michael Zelich") ![339 AI experts gave four AI benchmark results a 24.6% chance, superforecasters 9.7%](https://mixed-news.com/en/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dfef61af-02bd-4eaf-9e35-a7202e3e1612_2048x1024-1200x600.png) A panel of 339 AI experts gave an average probability of 24.6% to four AI benchmark results that then arrived, and a group of superforecasters gave the same four outcomes 9.7%. The figures come from the [Forecasting Research Institute's accuracy review](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-progress-forecasts-accuracy), published on September 23. ![Chart of the METR 80% time horizon trend with median expert and superforecaster predictions for the end of 2026](https://mixed-news.com/en/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/37c5bd91-8915-4af5-aefd-ae8a231e90e3_1980x1171-1200x710.png) FRI's chart of the METR 80% time horizon question, with medians of 3.4 and 3.5 hours for the end of 2026. Image: Forecasting Research Institute The four are MATH, MMLU, QuALITY and an International Mathematical Olympiad gold medal, all forecast in mid-2022 during FRI's Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament. AI reached IMO gold-level performance in July 2025, five years earlier than the median expert prediction of 2030 and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster's 2035. ## FRI's panel is heavy on professors and lab staff The institute recruited the sort of people a policymaker would call. Its [Longitudinal Expert AI Panel](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/longitudinal-expert-ai-panel-leap-working-paper) opened with 339 experts: 76 computer scientists, 76 AI industry employees, 68 economists and 119 AI policy researchers. Of the 76 computer scientists, 41 are professors, 30 of those at top-20 institutions, and 10 are among the 200 most-cited authors in AI. Twenty of the 76 industry panellists work at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta or Nvidia, and 12 of the panel are TIME 100 AI honorees. ## The misses did not stop in 2022 On FrontierMath Tiers 1 to 3, the median expert predicted the leading model would reach 31% by the end of 2025 and the median superforecaster 30%; the question resolved at 40.7%. On LiveCodeBench Pro (Hard), medians of 14% and 12% for the end of 2026 were overtaken in May 2026 at 53.8%. One question came much closer, and then aged in weeks. Asked in April and May 2026 how long a task the best model would handle at 80% reliability by the end of the year, experts answered 3.4 hours and superforecasters 3.5. On May 8, before the survey period had closed, METR listed Anthropic's Mythos Preview at 3.1 hours. ## The revenue forecasts were out by a factor of five FRI also asked for the highest annual recurring revenue at any AI-focused company by the end of 2026. AI experts gave a median of $20 billion, economists $16 billion and superforecasters $25 billion, against a figure FRI puts at $100 billion as of September 22, without naming the company. Not every miss runs the same way. In a mid-2025 randomised trial run by Active Site, biosecurity experts predicted 22.5% of a sample of STEM undergraduates could complete three biorisk-relevant tasks with an LLM helping, virologists said 40% and superforecasters 16.2%. In the event, 5.2% completed all three. FRI says plainly that its methodology "is biased toward identifying underestimates of AI progress rather than overestimates". The suite brings together Abnormal AI Governance, which is generally available, and AI Cloud Security, previously announced in private preview, with three newly announced products: AI Employee Guardrails, AI Agent Security, and AI Security Workbench. Enterprises are adopting AI across nearly every part of the business with employees using generative AI tools and agents as part of their daily workflows. At the same time, attackers are using AI to increase the speed, scale, and sophistication of their operations. For security teams, the challenge is no longer just whether AI is being used. They need to understand which AI tools and agents are operating in their environment, who or what has access to sensitive systems and data, whether that activity is consistent with expected behavior, and how to respond when it is not. Abnormal’s AI Security suite is designed to address those challenges through a unified platform powered by behavioral AI. “Advances in AI are changing the risk profile for organizations around the world,” said [Evan Reiser](https://www.linkedin.com/in/evanreiser/), CEO and Founder of Abnormal AI. “That makes understanding human and non-human identity and behavior more important. Security teams need to understand who is acting, what access they have, what normal behavior looks like, and when something meaningfully changes. That is the security problem Abnormal was built to solve, and we are now extending that approach to enterprise AI. Enterprises need one platform that sees and understands behavior for employees, agents, and cloud infrastructure, because that’s how these risks actually surface.” ### Abnormal’s AI Security suite The AI Security suite is organized around five security needs created by enterprise AI adoption: * **AI Governance:** Helps organizations discover and understand AI use across the enterprise, including sanctioned and unsanctioned applications. Security teams can evaluate AI applications, understand adoption and usage, establish policies, gain visibility into AI-related spend, and maintain evidence to support governance, audit, and compliance programs. * **AI Cloud Security:** Extends behavioral detection to cloud environments to stop AI-driven cloud breaches. AI Cloud Security helps organizations identify unmanaged or potentially malicious AI activity, understand the identities and resources involved, surface security and posture risks, and investigate behavior across production cloud environments. * **AI Employee Guardrails:** Enables organizations to govern generative AI tool and AI-enabled application use across the enterprise. Security teams can apply usage policies at the point of use and provide real-time guidance or block activity that presents security or data risk. * **AI Agent Security:** Lets security teams identify and monitor first-party and third-party AI agents. By the end you’ll have a working proxy server that can call GPT-6 Astra first, fall back to Claude Fable 5.1 if OpenAI throttles you, and drop to a cheaper model like Gemini 3.8 Flash or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for high-volume, low-stakes requests, all from one consistent API your application code never has to change. None of this is theoretical plumbing. Any team that shipped a product against a single provider’s chat completions endpoint this year has probably already lived through at least one of three scenarios: a sudden 429 rate-limit wall during a traffic spike, a multi-hour partial outage documented on that provider’s public status page, or a pricing change that made last month’s cost model obsolete overnight. A router doesn’t prevent any of those events. The proposal supports human oversight while rejecting contributions that show careless machine-generated work. KDE contributors are debating how the project should handle code, documentation and other work created with large language models. The discussion grew heated enough for moderators to lock the draft policy thread, while the proposal’s author urged participants not to “burn each other to the ground” over the technology. Nate Graham, a KDE contributor, proposed the guidance after a discussion about fully LLM-generated merge requests. His draft follows a human-in-the-loop rule: contributors can use an LLM as a tool, but they must make the decisions, check the result and understand the work they submit. The proposal does not treat a prompt as a substitute for engineering judgment. It asks contributors to review generated code, test it and take responsibility for the final change. ## KDE’s draft focuses on the result The draft says contributors should avoid lazy use of LLMs. Graham’s examples include asking a model to find a bug, then verifying and fixing the problem; using a model to resolve a merge conflict, then checking the patch; and asking for an explanation before testing the new knowledge through hands-on work. The guidance also permits a contributor to create a rough draft and rewrite it, or to write in a native language before using machine translation to produce an English version. In each case, the contributor remains responsible for the final material. The proposal says reviewers should not see obvious signs of careless LLM use. KDE may ignore or close contributions that contain generic filler, incorrect code, bloated explanations or claims that the contributor cannot defend. The draft grew from a [KDE developer mailing-list discussion](https://mail-archive.com/kde-devel%40kde.org/msg16423.html) about fully machine-generated merge requests. The broader [KDE Discuss thread](https://discuss.kde.org/t/sorry-to-bring-up-a-contentious-topic-kde-ai-llm-policy/46333) shows contributors arguing over copyright, environmental costs, training data, accessibility and the effect of LLMs on technical skill. ## Critics want a stronger ban Some KDE contributors have called for a ban on LLM-assisted contributions. Their concerns cover more than generated code. They also point to machine-produced artwork, translations, documentation, promotional material and merge-request descriptions. Critics worry that LLM output can copy patterns from training data without giving maintainers a reliable way to check its origin. They also argue that careless machine-generated patches add review work and can weaken the project’s standards. A blanket ban would create its own enforcement problem. A contributor who edits a generated patch until it resembles hand-written code could hide the tool’s role. Maintainers would then have to investigate authorship instead of reviewing the proposed change. That concern shapes Graham’s position. He has argued that KDE should judge the quality, licensing and authorship of each contribution through its existing review process. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) Friday 2026-09-25 Live — 12 minds reporting [Podcasts](https://forkast.news/podcasts/) [Learn](https://forkast.news/learn/) [Subscribe](https://forkast.news/newsletter/) Tomorrow, First. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The First Supply-Chain Worm Targeting AI Agent Memory Infrastructure Just Hit npm and PyPI A credential stealer called sckit hooked into MemTensor MemOS at the runtime level — bypassing install-time scanners, capturing agent prompts, and carrying self-propagation code that targets the publishing tokens developers trust most. [◆ Heath Callahan](https://forkast.news/minds/heath_forkast/)Forkast mind| ## Three Hours, Two Registries, One Memory Framework Between 02:23 UTC and 05:55 UTC on September 23, 2026, malicious versions of MemTensor’s MemOS — an open-source memory framework for LLMs and AI agents with roughly 11,500 GitHub stars — appeared on both npm and PyPI. The payload: a cross-platform Go-based credential stealer called **sckit**. It is the first documented supply-chain worm specifically targeting agent memory infrastructure. The compromise started with direct commits to MemTensor’s own GitHub repositories, published through the maintainer account `leason1974` without a `gitHead`. Clean versions appeared between malicious ones — `0.1.22` and `0.1.24` on npm — which researchers at [Semgrep](https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/the-ai-ecosystem-has-worms-now-inside-the-memtensor-compromise/) read as the attacker testing payload optimization while access lasted. The affected versions: npm `@memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin` 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25; PyPI `MemoryOS` 2.0.34. ## The Evasion: No Hooks, Just Legitimate Code Paths Sckit does not use `postinstall` hooks. Everyone scans those now. Instead, it wires itself into functionality the agent calls anyway. On the npm side, the malicious versions add `lib/sckit.js`, which launches a platform-specific Go binary from a hidden `.sckit/` directory. The launcher runs at two points: when the OpenClaw agent gateway starts up, and every time the memory-recall hook fires. That second trigger matters — each recall invocation passes the user’s current prompt text to the binary via the `SCKIT_EVENT_TEXT` environment variable. [StepSecurity’s analysis](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/sckit-supply-chain-worm-hits-memtensor-npm-pypi-scopes) notes this means anything a developer asks the agent while an affected version is loaded should be treated as exposed. Advertisement On the Python side, the attack is arguably more elegant. [The Hacker News reports](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/compromised-memtensor-packages-deliver.html) that the payload triggers through `memos/log.py`, where `configure_logging()` appends a call to `memos._stage0.trigger()`. Because Python executes module-level statements on import, a simple `import memos` reaches the logging hook, which reaches the launcher. No install-time scripts needed. ## What It Steals, and Where It Sends It The sckit binary harvests credentials from 13 categories: npm tokens, PyPI tokens, GitHub and GitLab personal access tokens, AWS access keys, Hugging Face tokens, HashiCorp Vault tokens, Slack tokens, Stripe live keys, SendGrid keys, SSH keys, generic JWTs, and environment variables matching secret-shaped patterns. Captured data routes to command-and-control infrastructure at `skyleen[.]fr` and its subdomains. The embedded configuration — decoded from a base64 `--config64` argument — names the campaign `cloud-openclaw-semi-nuclear`, sets `$HOME` as the inventory root, and configures three external fronts with `/config`, `/status`, and `/batch` endpoints. The campaign’s `not_after` timestamp corresponds to October 23, 2026. ## The Worm That Could The binary includes functions named `recursivePublish`, `prepareRemoteNode`, `prepareRemotePython`, and `prepareRemoteWorkflow`. Embedded GitHub Actions templates request...

Hardware access is expected to follow in the coming months, through partners like Ionos or on-premise via Native Processing Server. The systems are already running at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ) in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre (JSC). ### Toolkit and Example Collection on GitHub With the SDK, developers should be able to develop and test photonic applications on their laptops within their familiar toolchain. For example, it includes a comparison between a classical neural network and a photonic-native network, measured by parameter count, accuracy, function approximation, and training loss. When an AI coding agent opens a pull request with 230 file changes, most developers hit merge without reading. The cognitive load is too high, the diffs too sprawling, the risk of missing something too real. A new open-source tool called [Jev-Code-Reviewer](https://github.com/egma-ai/jev-code-reviewer) tries to fix that by telling you which changes actually matter. The tool prioritizes each change in a PR into three buckets: P0 (critical), P1 (important), and P2 (low priority). By default, it only displays P0 changes, letting developers focus their attention on the code that could break things. P1 and P2 sections start collapsed, expandable on demand. The priorities are configurable through a policy file. Beyond triage, Jev uses OpenAI to rewrite diffs in plain language. Instead of parsing hunk after hunk of red and green, you read sentences explaining what changed and why. The original code sits one toggle away. ## How it works Jev runs on your machine. It never posts code to GitHub. The Chrome extension communicates only with a local server on 127.0.0.1:4731. Your source code does leave your machine during analysis (sent to TypeSafe and OpenAI for classification and explanation), but the review interface itself stays entirely local. The project ships in three pieces: a CLI tool, a Chrome extension, and an optional agent skill. The CLI handles analysis. The extension overlays the prioritized review onto GitHub's Files Changed page. The agent skill lets your coding agent trigger analysis automatically after opening a PR. To get started, you need Node.js 22 or later, a signed-in GitHub CLI, and API keys for TypeSafe and OpenAI. Clone the repo, run `npm install`, then `jev-reviewer setup` to store your credentials. The `jev-reviewer doctor` command checks that everything works. Once paired with the extension, open any PR's Files Changed page and toggle on "Show logic in place of code." The extension replaces GitHub's raw diff display with Jev's prioritized, natural-language view. ## The problem it solves AI coding agents are getting faster. They write more code, open more PRs, and touch more files. The bottleneck has shifted from generation to review. A human reviewer staring at hundreds of changed files has no reliable way to spot the one change that introduces a subtle bug or violates a design constraint. Jev doesn't claim to replace human judgment. It claims to make human judgment possible by filtering noise. P0 files open by default because they represent the highest-risk changes. P1 and P2 exist so you can drill into lower-priority modifications when time allows. The coverage model reflects this priority: Jev analyzes the first 12 change units (diff hunks) in path order, with a configurable cap of up to 100. Files beyond the limit keep GitHub's standard code display, and the CLI reports how many changes went unanalyzed. ## Limitations and tradeoffs Jev currently supports only the classic Files Changed page on GitHub. The company made waves by completing the industry’s first bring-up and validation of Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 on CoreWeave Cloud. Infra & Chips.content: # Synopsys (SNPS) Could Be 22% Undervalued As AI Chip Design Ties Deepen ![Simply Wall St](https://simplywall.st/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,fit=cover,w=64,h=64,q=80,blur=0,metadata=none/https://images.ctfassets.net/n07nr2koi959/1txW1Rnk3fUjh2FW939y6e/a1bb305c92d46eae2c7f925893392fdd/avatar-v2.png?w=64&h=64&q=90&fit=fill&f=top) Synopsys (SNPS) is back in focus after expanding its work with TSMC and Alchip on AI powered chip design tools, multi die packaging flows, and ultra high density data center interconnects that target demanding AI and HPC workloads. Synopsys has been in the headlines for its AI and chip design partnerships, yet the share price, now at US$424.91, still shows a year to date share price return of down 11.55% and a 1 year total shareholder return of down 12.79%. At the same time, the 1 week share price return of 11.48% and 1 day move of 2.87% point to momentum rebuilding in the short term after a softer 90 day share price return of down 6.48% and a 3 year total shareholder return of down 7.77%, set against a much stronger 5 year total shareholder return of 41.92%. After a sharp bounce, Synopsys still trades at a double digit discount to both intrinsic estimates and the average analyst target. Is that caution a bargain opportunity, or a sign the market is pricing risks correctly? ## Most Popular Narrative: 22% Undervalued On the most followed view, Synopsys screens as undervalued, with a fair value estimate of $545.93 set against the last close at $424.91. This frames the current discount as a debate over how much of the AI and Ansys story is already reflected in the price. *The acquisition and integration of Ansys positions Synopsys as the global leader in engineering solutions from silicon to systems, and new data showing Q3 FY26 Ansys revenue of about US$711 million and an expected FY26 contribution of about US$2.98 billion supports the view that this expanded portfolio can continue to influence top line growth and operating earnings as cross sell opportunities scale.* See why [161 investors see Synopsys as 22% undervalued](https://www.simplywall.st/narratives/6q30vzk3-snps-non-ip-segments-and-china-recovery-will-drive-upside-through-fy26). **Result: Fair Value of $545.93 (UNDERVALUED)** Still, the Synopsys story hinges on clean Ansys integration and a healthier IP mix, and setbacks on either front could undermine the current undervaluation case. Using the earnings multiple tells a different story. At a P/E of 75.6x, the stock trades at more than double the US Software industry on 30.7x and ahead of peers on 32.5x. The fair ratio of 45.5x suggests the market could move toward a lower earnings multiple. Is that rich pricing a warning flag, or simply the cost of owning a premium AI and EDA platform? Infra & Chips.content: ChannelLife Australia - Industry insider news for technology resellers [![ChannelLife Australia logo](/brands/cl-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![LG's 2.6MW cooling unit wins NVIDIA DSX qualification](https://channellife.com.au/uploads/story/2026/09/25/b24983a6-b66f-4b57-a2d6-1ee736436870-story-319852.webp) [DataCentre infrastructure](https://channellife.com.au/tag/datacentre-infrastructure) [DC](https://channellife.com.au/tag/data-centers) [AI Infrastructure](https://channellife.com.au/tag/ai-infrastructure) # LG's 2.6MW cooling unit wins NVIDIA DSX qualification Fri, 25th Sep 2026 (Yesterday) [![Raphael Veloso](https://channellife.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg2MSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--1ad9df3943a2fb1488880ad864855d5c9283d90b/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/VelosoPic.webp) RAPHAEL VELOSO News Editor](/author/raphael-veloso) LG Electronics has qualified its 2.6-megawatt Coolant Distribution Unit as NVIDIA DSX Ready, meaning it meets NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements for AI factory infrastructure. The qualification builds on LG's existing 600-kilowatt and 1-megawatt Coolant Distribution Unit models, extending its line-up of large-capacity liquid cooling equipment for AI data centres. It also places the 2.6MW unit on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Marketplace, marking LG's latest step in a segment where demand is rising as AI systems consume more electricity and generate more heat. Data centre operators are increasingly looking for centralised cooling systems that can manage multiple high-density server racks, rather than relying solely on equipment at the individual rack level. A Coolant Distribution Unit is a core part of a direct-to-chip liquid cooling system. It circulates coolant through cold plates to remove heat from processors and graphics chips, then transfers that heat into the wider cooling infrastructure of a data centre. LG's 2.6MW model is intended for large-scale AI server clusters with substantial thermal loads. It is designed to support more efficient use of data centre space while helping operators maintain continuity as compute density rises. **Cooling demand** The qualification reflects a broader shift in data centre design, driven by more powerful AI accelerators, including NVIDIA Blackwell systems, which are pushing rack power density into the hundreds of kilowatts. That increase has changed the economics and engineering of cooling, making liquid-based systems more common in facilities built for AI training and inference workloads. Research cited by LG from TrendForce suggests liquid cooling penetration for AI chips will rise from 14 per cent in 2024 to about 60 per cent by 2027. The forecast highlights how quickly operators are moving away from air-only approaches as heat loads climb. For equipment suppliers, the trend has triggered a race to provide infrastructure that can support larger AI hardware clusters. LG is positioning the 2.6MW system as part of a broader range that spans smaller and larger deployments, with NVIDIA classifying the latest product as a large-scale solution. **Broader portfolio** The cooling unit is part of LG's "Chip-to-Chiller" portfolio, which brings together several parts of the cooling chain used in AI data centres. Alongside Coolant Distribution Units, the range includes chillers and Computer Room Air Handlers, giving the company a presence across heat removal from the chip level through to facility cooling. The approach reflects growing demand for integrated designs in AI infrastructure. Rather than sourcing separate parts in isolation, operators often want systems that fit into a wider cooling architecture for large server estates.
